method: The lift is the smaller of two limits: the tonnes the cargo holds can take at the cargo's stowage factor, grain capacity divided by the stowage factor, and the deadweight cargo capacity the ship may load. When the hold limit is lower the ship is space-limited and deadweight is left unused; when the deadweight is lower the ship is weight-limited and hold space is left empty; when the two agree the cargo exactly fills the holds at the deadweight. Cargo volume is the lift times the stowage factor and hold use is that volume as a percentage of grain capacity. The worked examples in the reference follow the same rule: 70,000 m3 of grain capacity and 55,000 t of deadweight lift 55,000 t of phosphate at 0.90 m3/t, because the hold limit of 77,777.8 t is above the deadweight, and 47,619 t of barley at 1.47 m3/t, because the hold limit falls below it. The reference table of typical stowage factors (iron ore 0.40, grain 1.30, coal 1.40, woodchips 2.50) supplies the comparison rows, and the cargo's own stowage factor row is dropped when it repeats one of them. The stowage factor is the volume one tonne occupies in the hold including normal stowage losses, so no separate broken-stowage percentage is applied on top of it. Grain capacity is 1 to 2,000,000 m3, deadweight cargo capacity 1 to 1,000,000 t and the stowage factor 0.05 to 20 m3/t. The page is a planning estimate, not a loading instruction: actual loading follows the ship's stability booklet, load line and cargo declaration and the terminal's measured weights, and trim, list, tank capacity, deadweight at the sailing draft, cargo density limits and segregation rules are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Stowage factor: cubic metres of hold space one tonne of cargo occupies, with the table of typical stowage factors and the worked grain-capacity and deadweight examples the lift rule follows
